studies.title: Purify, Remember, Then Pray
studies.meaning: The contrast is between two verbs of avoidance and approach. One turns aside from the reminder and is described entering a fire where neither death nor life is available, a condition the classical readers dwell on because it removes the last exit. Then a single line names success, and it has three parts: purifying oneself, remembering the name, and praying. The order runs from the inside outward.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and among the early surahs. It follows a promise that the one addressed will be eased toward what is easy, and an instruction to remind if reminding is useful. No specific occasion is reported. The classical sources report that this surah was among those recited in the congregational prayers, so its short lines were among the first many people learned.

keyTerms.note: Built on the word for a side, so the image is keeping something to one side of you rather than refusing it outright. It describes a person who never argues with the reminder and never comes near it.
A superlative from the word for hardship and misery, the same root behind the name given to an unlucky life. It is set against the word for success two lines later, and the pair frames the passage.

From a root that carries both cleansing and increase, and behind the word for the yearly share of wealth. Purifying and growing are the same verb, so removing something is described as a way of getting larger.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fire in Arabia was a small, precious thing. Households kept an ember alive because starting one was work, and a traveller navigated at night partly by the fires of settlements. Nobody in that world had seen a large fire that could not be escaped. The description of a state in which a person neither dies nor lives had no equivalent in their experience, and the language reflects that by refusing to describe it further.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah ends by saying that what has just been said is in the earlier scriptures, and it names the pages of Abraham and Moses. The classical commentators discuss how far back the reference reaches, some limiting it to the last few lines and some extending it to the whole chapter, and the disagreement is recorded without a decision.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Success is given a definition in one line, and it is short enough to be checked. Purification comes first, then remembrance, then prayer, which puts the inward work before the outward act rather than after it. The failure described just before is also worth noting: it is not opposition. The person simply steps around the reminder, which makes avoidance rather than argument the condition being warned against.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for purification and the same verdict of success, applied to the soul directly.
Names the reason people step around the reminder, a preference stated plainly two lines later.
Joins the same two elements, remembrance and prayer, and makes one the purpose of the other.

studies.applyIt: Take the three items in the last line and do them in that order once today, in about four minutes. Remove something first: an unkind thought you were rehearsing, a grudge you were about to feed. Then say the name of God once. Then pray. The order is the instruction, and most people do it backwards.
